source.text: Εἶπεν οὖν πάλιν αὐτοῖς· Ἐγὼ ὑπάγω καὶ ζητήσετέ με, καὶ ἐν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ὑμῶν ἀποθανεῖσθε· ὅπου ἐγὼ ὑπάγω ὑμεῖς οὐ δύνασθε ἐλθεῖν.

records.literal_gloss: Said therefore again to them, "I go away and you will seek me, and in the sin of you you will die; where I go you not are able to come."

en.L: So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them again, "I go away, and you will seek {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and you will die in your sin. Where I go, you cannot come."
en.B: Once more {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said to them, "I am going away, and you will search for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and you will die in your sin. You cannot come where I am going."
en.R: Then Jesus spoke to them again. "I am going away," {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said. "You will look for {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and you will die still guilty of your sin. You are not able to come where I am going."

decisions.choice: I go away: his departure to the Father through his death
decisions.reason: As in 7:33, this verb is John's word for Jesus's return to the one who sent him (13:3; 16:5). He has said where he goes (8:14); his hearers do not know (8:22).

decisions.choice: die in your sin: die with the sin still on you, unforgiven
alternatives: die because of your sin
decisions.reason: To die in one's sin is a phrase from the Scriptures for dying under the guilt of sin, with nothing done to remove it (Ezekiel 3:18-20; 18:24). The point is not the cause of death but the state in which they die: cut off from the one who takes away the sin of the world (1:29).

decisions.choice: sin, singular: the one sin of refusing him
alternatives: a collective word for all their sins
decisions.reason: Here Jesus says "sin"; in 8:24 he says "sins" twice. The singular most likely names the root sin of unbelief, which 16:9 calls sin ("because they do not believe in me") and which leaves all other sins in place (3:18, 36; 9:41). The plural in 8:24 then names the sins that unbelief leaves unforgiven. The singular may also be simply collective; the sense is close either way.

decisions.choice: you will seek me: too late, and not to find life
decisions.reason: In 7:34 Jesus said they would seek him and not find him. Here he says what that means: they will look for him when he is gone and die in their sin. He says to his disciples that they too cannot come where he goes (13:33), but promises to come back and take them to himself (13:36; 14:3); to these hearers he makes no such promise.

decisions.choice: going away, search for (B); look for, still guilty of your sin (R)
alternatives: go away, seek, die in your sin (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the same words as in 7:33-34 so the echo stays visible, and put "where I am going" after the verb, as there. Readable explains the phrase "die in your sin" (meaning decision m2).

source.text: ἔλεγον οὖν οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι· Μήτι ἀποκτενεῖ ἑαυτὸν ὅτι λέγει· Ὅπου ἐγὼ ὑπάγω ὑμεῖς οὐ δύνασθε ἐλθεῖν;

records.literal_gloss: Were saying therefore the Jews, "Not will he kill himself, that he says, 'Where I go you not are able to come'?"

en.L: So the Jews were saying, "He will not kill {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}, will {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}, since {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, 'Where I go, you cannot come'?"
en.B: At this the Jewish leaders said, "Surely {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is not going to kill {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}? Is that why {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, 'You cannot come where I am going'?"
en.R: The Jewish leaders said, "Surely {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is not going to kill {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}! Is that why {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} says, 'You are not able to come where I am going'?"

decisions.choice: the Jews: the hostile hearers in the temple, the authorities and those siding with them
alternatives: the listeners in the temple generally
the Jewish people in general
decisions.reason: The scene goes on from 8:13-20, where Jesus answers the Pharisees in the temple treasury, and from 7:35, where "the Jews" took his words about going away in the same mocking way. The speakers are those who reject him and seek his death (7:1; 8:37, 40). John does not say they are only officials; others in the temple who sided with them may be included. It is not the people as a whole: many who hear him believe (8:30), and Jesus himself is a Jew.

decisions.choice: a question that expects no, while raising the thought in mockery
decisions.reason: The question opens with a negative particle that looks for "no" but leaves the idea hanging: "He will not kill himself, will he?" The same particle introduces the Samaritan woman's hesitant question in 4:29. Here the tone is scornful: if no one can follow him, perhaps he means to go where no decent person goes.

decisions.choice: irony: he will indeed give up his life, but not as they mean
decisions.reason: In 7:35 they guessed he would go to the Greeks; now they guess he will take his own life, which was held to be a grave wrong. Again they speak more truly than they know: he will lay down his life of his own accord (10:17-18), though it is they who will put him to death (8:28, 37), and his death is the way he goes to the Father.

decisions.choice: since he says: the reason they offer for their guess
decisions.reason: The word that joins the two parts gives the ground for their question: they reason from his words, "Where I go, you cannot come", which they repeat as he said them in 8:21.

decisions.choice: the Jewish leaders
alternatives: the Jews (Literal)
decisions.reason: Where the word means the authorities and those with them, Balanced and Readable name them, as at 7:35 (see the book's terms). The footnote gives the word John wrote.

decisions.choice: Surely ... not ...? Is that why (B); Surely ... not ...! (R)
alternatives: one question with a tag (Literal)
decisions.reason: English shows that "no" is expected (meaning decision m2) with "surely ... not", and splits the long question in two. The words they quote are given as each level gave them in 8:21.

source.text: καὶ ἔλεγεν αὐτοῖς· Ὑμεῖς ἐκ τῶν κάτω ἐστέ, ἐγὼ ἐκ τῶν ἄνω εἰμί· ὑμεῖς ἐκ τούτου τοῦ κόσμου ἐστέ, ἐγὼ οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου τούτου.

records.literal_gloss: And he was saying to them, "You from the [things] below are, I from the [things] above am; you of this the world are, I not am of the world this.

en.L: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was saying to them, "You are from the [places] below; I am from the [places] above. You are of this world; I am not of this world.
en.B: He went on to say to them, "You come from below; I come from above. You are from this world; I am not from this world.
en.R: Jesus told them, "You come from down here below. I come from heaven above. You come from this world. I do not come from this world.

decisions.choice: below and above: the earthly realm and the realm of God
alternatives: below as the underworld
decisions.reason: The two words name where one comes from: the earth, or heaven where God is. John the Baptist made the same contrast in 3:31 ("the one who comes from above is above all"), and Jesus told Nicodemus that he came down from heaven (3:13). "Below" does not mean the world of the dead; it is this world, as the second half of the verse says.

decisions.choice: this world: human life organized apart from God and set against him
alternatives: the created order
all humanity, loved by God
decisions.reason: Key term. John uses "world" for the creation (1:10a), for humanity whom God loves (3:16), and for humanity that refuses God (7:7; 15:18-19). "This world" here is the last: the order to which his hearers belong in their unbelief. Jesus says the same of his disciples later, that they are not of the world as he is not (15:19; 17:14, 16), so the point is not birthplace but where a person's life comes from.

decisions.choice: from ... of: where one comes from, and so what one is
decisions.reason: The same preposition is used in all four clauses. It gives origin, and in John origin shapes character: what is born of the flesh is flesh (3:6), the one from the earth speaks of the earth (3:31). Because they belong to this world, they cannot come where he goes (8:21).

decisions.choice: from the [places] below/above (L); come from (B, R); down here, heaven (R)
alternatives: You are from below; I am from above
decisions.reason: The Greek has "from the [things] below"; Literal brackets "places" so the article stays visible. Balanced and Readable use "come from" in all four clauses, since the point is origin (meaning decision m3). Readable says where "above" is, heaven, as in 3:13 and 3:31, and says "down here" for below.

source.text: εἶπον οὖν ὑμῖν ὅτι ἀποθανεῖσθε ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν· ἐὰν γὰρ μὴ πιστεύσητε ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι, ἀποθανεῖσθε ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν.

records.literal_gloss: I said therefore to you that you will die in the sins of you; if for not you believe that I am, you will die in the sins of you."

en.L: So I said to you that you will die in your sins; for if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins."
en.B: That is why I told you that you will die in your sins. For unless you believe that I am, you will die in your sins."
en.R: That is why I told you that you will die still guilty of your sins. If you do not believe that I am, you will die still guilty of your sins."

decisions.choice: I am: the words with which God names himself, said by Jesus of himself; the claim includes being the one from above whom the Father sent
alternatives: a plain "I am he": I am the one I claim to be (the one from above, the Christ)
the divine name alone, with no thought of his claims in the context
decisions.reason: Jesus says "I am" with nothing after it, and his hearers at once ask, "Who are you?" (8:25), so no predicate is plain from the context, as it is in 4:26 (the Messiah) and 6:20 (it is I). The words are those God uses of himself in the Greek of Isaiah: "that you may know and believe ... that I am" (Isaiah 43:10; also 43:25; 45:18; 46:4), echoing "I am who I am" (Exodus 3:14) and "See now that I, I am he" (Deuteronomy 32:39). Isaiah 43:10 joins knowing and believing to these words as 8:24 and 8:28 do. In the same speech Jesus says he is from above (8:23), and 8:58 ends with "before Abraham was, I am". So the echo of God's name is uppermost, with the claim to be the one from above held within it. Some take it more plainly as "I am he", the one I say I am; that reading is given in the footnote. Marked uncertain because both senses are present and the weight between them is a judgment.

decisions.choice: your sins, plural: the sins left unforgiven
decisions.reason: Jesus repeats what he said in 8:21, but now with the plural. Unbelief, the one sin of 8:21 (meaning decision m3 there), leaves all their sins in place; only the one who takes away the sin of the world can remove them (1:29).

decisions.choice: for if you do not believe: the condition that explains the warning
decisions.reason: "For" gives the reason for the warning just repeated. The warning is not final: it holds unless they believe. Believing is the way out of dying in sin, as eternal life is promised to the one who believes (3:16, 36; 5:24).

decisions.choice: that I am, with no "he" supplied (also in 8:28)
alternatives: that I am he
that I am who I claim to be
decisions.reason: Because the echo of God's name is uppermost (meaning decision m1), every level keeps the bare words, here and in 8:28, as 8:58 will. Supplying "he" would settle the sense on the plain reading. The English reads as unfinished, as the Greek did to those who heard it (8:25). The footnote gives "that I am he".

decisions.choice: die still guilty of your sins
alternatives: die in your sins (Literal, Balanced)
decisions.reason: As in 8:21, Readable explains the phrase "die in your sins".

source.text: ἔλεγον οὖν αὐτῷ· Σὺ τίς εἶ;

records.literal_gloss: Were saying therefore to him, "You, who are you?"

en.L: So they were saying to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "You, who are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}?"

decisions.choice: an emphatic "you": a challenge
decisions.reason: The question puts "you" first for emphasis: "You, who are you?" After the bare "I am" of 8:24 they demand that he say plainly who he claims to be. The same question was put to John the Baptist (1:19), and in 10:24 they will demand, "If you are the Christ, tell us plainly."

decisions.choice: they: the same hearers as in 8:22
decisions.reason: The subject is not named. The speakers are those Jesus has just been addressing, the ones called "the Jews" in 8:22 (meaning decision m1 there).

decisions.choice: Just who are you? (B); Who are you, then? (R)
alternatives: You, who are you? (Literal)
decisions.reason: English cannot easily put "you" first twice; Balanced shows the challenge with "just", Readable with "then" (meaning decision m1).

source.text: εἶπεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Τὴν ἀρχὴν ὅ τι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν;

records.literal_gloss: Said to them the Jesus, "The beginning, what even I speak to you?

en.L: Jesus said to them, "Why do I even speak to you at all?
en.B: Jesus said to them, "Why am I even talking to you at all?
en.R: Jesus answered them, "Why do I even talk to you at all?

decisions.choice: a question: "Why do I even speak to you at all?"
alternatives: "What I have been telling you from the beginning" (a statement)
"I am what I have told you from the beginning"
"I am, first of all, what I am telling you"
decisions.reason: One of the hardest sentences in John. The SBLGNT prints it as a question, and this translation follows that. Read so, the opening words have a sense they often have in Greek, "at all", and the next word asks "why": Jesus declines to answer again a question his whole speech has answered, and goes on in 8:26 to say he has much more to say and judge. The early manuscripts had no punctuation, so a statement is also possible: the opening words can mean "from the beginning", and the next word "what", giving "what I have been telling you from the beginning" (compare 8:24, 28; 10:25). That reading gives a direct answer to "Who are you?", but it uses the opening words in a sense they rarely have without a preposition. Marked uncertain; the footnote gives the other readings.

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT text, without added words
alternatives: "I told you at the beginning what I am also telling you" (an early papyrus)
decisions.reason: One early papyrus of John adds "I told you" at the start, which makes the sentence a statement about what Jesus said at the beginning. The other manuscripts do not have it, and it looks like an attempt to make a hard sentence easier. A reviewer should check this note against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: talking (B); answered, talk (R)
alternatives: speak (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the everyday verb, keeping "even" and "at all" so the question keeps its weariness. Readable says "answered", since he is replying to their question.

source.text: πολλὰ ἔχω περὶ ὑμῶν λαλεῖν καὶ κρίνειν· ἀλλ’ ὁ πέμψας με ἀληθής ἐστιν, κἀγὼ ἃ ἤκουσα παρ’ αὐτοῦ ταῦτα λαλῶ εἰς τὸν κόσμον.

records.literal_gloss: Many things I have concerning you to speak and to judge; but the [one] having sent me true is, and I, the things which I heard from him, these things I speak into the world.

en.L: I have many things to speak and to judge concerning you; but the one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is true, and I, what I heard from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, these things I speak to the world."
en.B: I have much to say about you, and much to judge. But the one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is true, and I tell the world what I have heard from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."
en.R: There are many things I could say about you and many things I could judge. But the one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is real and true. I tell the world the things I have heard from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

decisions.choice: I have many things to say and judge: much that he could say against them
alternatives: I must say and judge many things
decisions.reason: "I have ... to say" means there is much he could say, and the pairing with "judge" shows it would be against them. He has authority to judge (5:22, 27), though he did not come to condemn (3:17; 8:15-16).

decisions.choice: but: he holds back and speaks only what the Father gives
decisions.reason: The "but" turns from what he could say about them to what he does say: not his own verdict, but the message of the one who sent him. Even so, his words carry judgment, because they are the true words of God (8:16; 12:48-49).

decisions.choice: true: truthful and reliable
decisions.reason: As in 3:33 and 7:28, the word means that the one who sent him speaks truly and can be relied on. What Jesus passes on is therefore true as well (8:14, 40).

decisions.choice: to the world: to humanity, openly
decisions.reason: Key term. He speaks what he heard into the world, to people at large, not in secret (18:20). The world here is humanity, the people God loves and to whom he sent his Son (3:16-17), not the hostile order of 8:23.

decisions.choice: I tell the world what I have heard (B, R); real and true, could (R)
alternatives: what I heard from him, these things I speak to the world (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the object after the verb, the usual English order. Readable says "could" to show these are things he holds back (meaning decision m1), and "real and true" as at 7:28.

source.text: οὐκ ἔγνωσαν ὅτι τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῖς ἔλεγεν.

records.literal_gloss: Not they knew that the Father to them he was speaking.

en.L: They did not know that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was speaking to them [of] the Father.
en.B: They did not understand that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was speaking to them about the Father.
en.R: They did not understand that Jesus was talking to them about God the Father.

decisions.choice: did not know: did not grasp, failed to recognize
decisions.reason: The verb means know or recognize. They heard him speak of "the one who sent me" (8:26) but did not grasp that he meant God the Father, though he had named the Father plainly in 8:18-19. The narrator's remark shows how deep their failure to understand goes (8:19, 43).

decisions.choice: the Father: the one he was speaking about
decisions.reason: "The Father" is the object of "was speaking" in the sense "speaking of": he was telling them about the Father. The tense describes what he had been doing all along.

decisions.choice: understand (B, R); Jesus, God the Father (R)
alternatives: know (Literal)
decisions.reason: "Understand" says in plain English what the verb means here (meaning decision m1). Readable names Jesus and says "God the Father" so the reader sees who "the one who sent me" is; the narrator, not the hearers, knows this.

source.text: εἶπεν οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ὅταν ὑψώσητε τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, τότε γνώσεσθε ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι, καὶ ἀπ’ ἐμαυτοῦ ποιῶ οὐδέν, ἀλλὰ καθὼς ἐδίδαξέν με ὁ πατὴρ ταῦτα λαλῶ.

records.literal_gloss: Said therefore the Jesus, "When you lift up the Son of the Man, then you will know that I am, and from myself I do nothing, but just as taught me the Father, these things I speak.

en.L: So Jesus said, "When you lift up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am, and [that] I do nothing from {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}, but just as the Father taught {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, these things I speak.
en.B: So Jesus said, "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am, and that I do nothing on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} own, but I say these things just as the Father taught {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.
en.R: So Jesus said, "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am. You will know that I do nothing just on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} own. The things I say are what the Father taught {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}.

decisions.choice: lift up: raise on the cross, and by that exalt
alternatives: only exalt
only put to death
decisions.reason: The verb means both to raise something high and to exalt someone. John says it points to the way Jesus would die (12:32-33), and 3:14 and 12:34 use it the same way. In the Greek of Isaiah 52:13 the LORD's servant "will be lifted up and glorified". The cross is where he is raised up and where he is glorified, so every level keeps "lift up" with both senses.

decisions.choice: you will lift him up: his hearers will put him to death, and his death will show who he is
decisions.reason: Jesus says that they will do the lifting up: those who seek to kill him (8:37, 40) will hand him over to be crucified (19:15-16). His death will not be his defeat but the moment that reveals him. "Then you will know" may mean that some will come to see the truth after the cross, or that they will know it too late, to their judgment; John leaves both open (compare 12:32 and 19:37).

decisions.choice: I am: as in 8:24, the words God uses of himself
alternatives: a plain "I am he": I am the one I claim to be
decisions.reason: See meaning decision m1 at 8:24. "You will know that I am" is close to Isaiah 43:10, "that you may know and believe ... that I am", where God speaks of himself. Here the knowing is tied to the cross, where the Son is glorified (12:23; 17:1). Marked uncertain as at 8:24; the footnote gives "that I am he".

decisions.choice: and that I do nothing on my own: still part of what they will know
alternatives: a separate statement: "And I do nothing on my own ..."
decisions.reason: The "and" most likely continues what they will know: that he is who he says, and that all he does and says comes from the Father. It could also begin a fresh statement; the sense is much the same. The words repeat 5:19, 30 and 7:16-17.

decisions.choice: lift up / lifted up, with no "on the cross"; that I am, with no "he"
alternatives: lifted up on the cross (Readable)
that I am he
decisions.reason: The book-wide choice keeps "lifted up" at every level, as at 3:14; adding "on the cross" would lose the exaltation (meaning decision m1). "That I am" is kept bare at every level, as at 8:24 (rendering decision r-en-1 there).

decisions.choice: on my own (B); just on my own, The things I say are what the Father taught me (R)
alternatives: from myself (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "on my own", as at 5:19 and 5:30. Readable breaks the sentence into three and repeats "you will know" so the link is clear (meaning decision m4).

source.text: καὶ ὁ πέμψας με μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἐστιν· οὐκ ἀφῆκέν με μόνον, ὅτι ἐγὼ τὰ ἀρεστὰ αὐτῷ ποιῶ πάντοτε.

records.literal_gloss: And the [one] having sent me with me is; not he left me alone, because I the things pleasing to him do always."

en.L: And the one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has not left {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} alone, because I do the things pleasing to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} always."
en.B: The one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. He has not left {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} alone, because at all times I do what is pleasing to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."
en.R: The one who sent {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} is here with {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}. He has not left {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} on {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} own, because I always do what makes {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} glad."

decisions.choice: the one who sent me is with me: the Father's presence with the Son
decisions.reason: The Father who sent him has not sent him off alone: he is with him in all he does. Jesus says the same in 8:16 and again on the night before his death, "I am not alone, for the Father is with me" (16:32).

decisions.choice: has not left me alone: a settled fact
alternatives: did not leave me alone when he sent me
decisions.reason: The past tense looks at the whole of his mission: the Father has never left him on his own. It may look back to the sending itself; the meaning is much the same.

decisions.choice: because I always do what pleases him: the reason, and the sign, of the Father's presence
alternatives: only the evidence that the Father is with him
decisions.reason: The clause gives the reason the Father stays with him, but it also shows it: his perfect obedience is the mark of their unity (4:34; 5:30; 6:38). "Always" stands at the end for emphasis.

decisions.choice: at all times I do what is pleasing to him (B); always do what makes him glad, here with me, on my own (R)
alternatives: I do the things pleasing to him always (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the emphasis on "always" by putting "at all times" first. Readable uses everyday words for "pleasing" and "alone".

source.text: ταῦτα αὐτοῦ λαλοῦντος πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς αὐτόν.

records.literal_gloss: These things of him speaking, many believed in him.

en.L: While {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was speaking these things, many believed in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
en.B: While {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was saying this, many people came to believe in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
en.R: While Jesus was saying these things, many people believed in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: believed in him: a real but untested belief
decisions.reason: John uses the same words for true faith (3:16) and for belief that does not yet go deep (2:23-25; 7:31). The next verses test it: Jesus speaks to "the Jews who had believed him" (8:31), and by the end of the chapter they want to stone him (8:59). John does not say whether these are exactly the same people.

decisions.choice: while he was saying these things: at the time he spoke
decisions.reason: The construction gives the time and also suggests the cause: it was his words, not a sign, that led them to believe.

decisions.choice: many: from among his hearers
decisions.reason: "Many" is not defined. They come from the people listening in the temple, the same setting in which others mocked him (8:22). John often reports belief and hostility side by side (7:31-32; 10:19-21; 11:45-46).

decisions.choice: many people, came to believe (B); Jesus (R)
alternatives: many believed (Literal)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "many people"; Balanced says "came to believe" to show that their belief began here. Readable names Jesus at the start of a new paragraph.
